q1: SELECT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f1, (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f2 WHERE f1.drinker < f2.drinker AND f1.st = f2.st
q2: SELECT DISTINCT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM frequents AS f1, frequents AS f2 GROUP BY f1.drinker, f2.drinker HAVING SUM(f1.times_a_week) = SUM(f2.times_a_week)

q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM frequents AS f1, frequents AS f2 GROUP BY f1.drinker, f2.drinker HAVING SUM(f1.times_a_week) = SUM(f2.times_a_week)
explanation: Q1 compares aggregated sums of times_a_week for distinct drinkers using a self-join with equality on sums and a drinker order. Q2 cross-joins the Frequents table and uses HAVING SUM(f1.times_a_week) = SUM(f2.times_a_week), which effectively compares (sum1 * count2) = (sum2 * count1), not just sum1 = sum2. This leads to different results when sum1 = sum2 but count1 ≠ count2.
counterexample_dsp: Two drinkers with equal total times_a_week but different numbers of frequented bars. Q1 outputs the pair, Q2 does not.
